canonical_topic: Why natural gas spot and forward markets are distinct
definition: Natural gas spot markets (immediate delivery) and forward markets (future delivery) are priced by different logic because gas production, transportation, and storage must be arranged in advance.
core_idea: Spot prices reflect current on-hand supply and current demand, while forward prices reflect macro-level expectations of the average future supply-demand balance; because near-term supply can't be increased quickly while longer-term supply can, spot markets are substantially more volatile than forward markets.
key_points: If a shortage is expected weeks out, production can usually be increased to meet it.
If a shortage occurs today, there is no real way to get more supply immediately — moving large gas volumes into/out of storage or transferring supply from nearby areas on short notice is difficult.
Forward prices are set by macroeconomic, expected-average supply-demand relationships.
Spot prices are set by supply currently on hand and current consumer demand.
As a result, spot markets are substantially more volatile than forward markets.
relationships: Connects to the price-certainty term structure and to swing trades (storage-driven exploitation of spot volatility)
trading_implications: Traders can exploit spot volatility via storage arbitrage; forward-market participants face less near-term price uncertainty.
